title: Eisen v. Carlisle & Jacquelin (1974)
summary: The plaintiff could not shift certification-notice costs to defendants through a preliminary merits assessment.
notes:
Wal-Mart explains that Eisen’s language does not prohibit examining merits-related matters genuinely necessary to decide certification. The objection here concerned the preliminary merits inquiry used to allocate notice costs.

The Court also held that Rule 23(c)(2) requires individual notice to every class member who can be identified through reasonable effort (about 2,250,000 of the roughly six million odd-lot traders), and that 'nothing in either the language or history of Rule 23' authorizes a preliminary inquiry into the merits when deciding certification.

sections.Parties: Eisen sought to represent investors who made odd-lot stock trades on the New York Stock Exchange.
sections.Material Facts: The proposed class contained millions of investors, and roughly two million could be identified with reasonable effort. Eisen’s individual stake was small, while the cost of notice was substantial. The district court examined the apparent merits and allocated part of the notice expense to the defendants after concluding that the plaintiff was likely to prevail.
sections.Procedural History: The district court, after a preliminary merits hearing, ordered defendants to pay 90 percent of the notice cost; the Second Circuit reversed and ordered the class action dismissed. The Supreme Court (Powell, J.) agreed that Rule 23 authorizes neither a preliminary merits inquiry nor shifting notice costs to defendants, vacated the Second Circuit's judgment and remanded with directions to dismiss the class action as then defined.
sections.Issue: Could the court use a preliminary merits inquiry to shift the cost of notifying the class?
sections.Holding: No. The ordinary burden of financing the notice rested with the plaintiff, and the Rule did not authorize the allocation on that basis.
sections.Reasoning: The Rule’s notice protections for identifiable absent members were not displaced by the cost of compliance. Nor did a preliminary assessment of likely liability establish a procedural authority to charge the defendants. The chapter later distinguishes the tasks of identifying class members and the different setting of settlement or established liability.

learning.why: The plaintiff could not shift certification-notice costs to defendants through a preliminary merits assessment.

topics.cp-class-notice: Identifiable members of a Rule 23(b)(3) class were entitled to the specified individual notice. The representative plaintiff ordinarily bore the cost of certification notice.
topics.cp-class-certification: A preliminary assessment of merits did not authorize shifting notice costs to defendants.
topics.cp-frcp-23: The holding construes Rule 23(c)(2)'s individual-notice mandate and rejects any authority in Rule 23 for a preliminary merits hearing.
topics.cp-access: The case illustrates how notice cost can make a small-stakes negative-value class action impossible to maintain.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Douglas, joined by Justices Brennan and Marshall, dissented in part, arguing that the district court should be allowed to define smaller, manageable subclasses rather than being forced to require individual notice to all 2.25 million identifiable members.

mnemonic.rationale: Two million notices for an odd-lot class
